**I1** Economic Indicators - November 2011 ###### **All eyes have been on Europe in recent weeks; what is happening elsewhere?** The commodities markets concentrated more closely on the European markets in October than on the other major economies, although there have been some potentially significant developments, notably in the United States. Economic releases from the United States have, on the surface, been encouraging in the past few weeks and pointing to a nascent economic recovery. There is a risk attached to an optimistic assessment of these recent figures, however. ###### **Beware the possibility of a false dawn** Recent encouraging figures have included a 2.5% annualised quarter-on-quarter growth rate in the third quarter, within which was a 17.4% increase in business spending on equipment and software. This exceeded many economists’ expectations and (along with the poor reaction to the EU summit) boosted the dollar. This rate of growth is not, however, enough to be able to declare that the US economy is out of the doldrums. Unemployment stands at 9.1% and local economists suggest that for this to come down, the economy needs to be expanding at a rate of 3%. Consumer spending grew by 2.4% in the quarter and was also a key component of the overall rate of growth. Incomes are not growing at a commensurate rate, however. In September, for example, consumer purchases increased by 0.6% in September (month-on-month) against a 0.1% income rise. Keen pricesensitivity in some places** The focus of the physical market, which always attracts keen attention from market observers round the world, is the festival in the Hindu calendar that culminates in Diwali, which this year fell on 26th October. The festival of Diwali, the Goddess of Lights, is deemed to be the most auspicious day in the Hindu calendar for gift giving and gold has traditionally played a very important part in this. In the early part of this October bullion bankers were reporting heavy imports into India. There was an inference to be drawn here that the very sharp fall in price in late September had stimulated substantial physical demand and that some of this was designated for Diwali purchases. This suggested that the festival’s influence on the international market during the period of the festival itself might be less noticeable than in more normal times and this did turn out to be the case. The intraday price volatility also had its effect, of course, and sales of 22-carat gold pieces were sluggish. Retailers were suggesting an average drop of up to 20% by comparison with 2010 and were citing price volatility as a major reason for the fall. Unit weights were also lower and there were also signs of pricing wars that resulted in retailers discounting labour costs in order to try and maintain market share. Fabrication costs are another reason why, in times of high or volatile prices, some would-be gold jewellery purchasers tend to buy investment bars, often with a view to having those bars fabricated into finished pieces at a later stage.
